articles.title: Dozy Trump, 80, Slumps Over as He Struggles to Stay Awake
articles.description: Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images President Donald Trump slumped over in his chair and struggled to keep his eyes open in the Oval Office on Monday. Trump, 80, held an afternoon event to sign an executive order on childhood vaccines, where he was joined by top administration officials. But after the president called on others to speak, his eyes repeatedly fluttered shut as he sat behind his desk, and at one point, he even slumped over in his chair as others spoke. Read more at The Daily Beast.

articles.title: Mental health: one step forward and two steps back? | Letters
articles.description: Dr Kate Martin is encouraged by the new network of community clinics, while Prof Dr John R Ashton says the forthcoming mental health strategy is an opportunity to grasp the nettle, while Marjorie Wallace expresses concerns about plans to cut mental health jobs in the NHS It’s very encouraging to hear the announcement about the new network of community mental health clinics in England ( Editorial, 6 August ). The focus on early intervention is crucial, as it means that people can access treatment as early as possible, rather than waiting for their mental health to reach a crisis point. The centres should improve access, reaching people where they are. The government should make sure that they meaningfully involve people with lived experience of mental health problems to ensure the centres are co-designed and co-led with them. As your editorial says, parity between mental and physical healthcare became a policy goal in 2011. Mental health is an issue that unites us. According to new research, which we commissioned from More in Common, nearly three-quarters of the public believe that mental health is as important as physical health, most people are comfortable talking about it, and support for early intervention is high across the political spectrum. Three-quarters also say the government should do more to improve services. Continue reading...

articles.title: Breast cancer screening guidelines discriminate against families like mine | Brief letters
articles.description: Health concerns | Rubbish decisions | In sympathy | Funeral songs | Short illnesses Calls for changes to breast cancer guidelines for GPs are welcome ( Report, 4 August ). The existing guidelines are irrational. If your grandmother and mother have both had breast cancer, you are still not added to the intensified screening list unless an aunt or great-aunt or sister has also had breast cancer. Hence the system discriminates against families – like mine – with only one woman in a generation. Helen Hills York • It seems that Anna Tims’s correspondent committed the wrong environmental crime ( I was fined £500 after putting a coffee cup in a rubbish bag next to a full bin, 3 August ). articles.title: Preventing a Health Service Continuity Crisis in Syria - Donor Briefing Note - Evidence period: 2025 and 2026 Impact of Underfunding of Health Sector Syria June 2026
articles.description: Country: Syrian Arab Republic Sources: Health Cluster, World Health Organization Please refer to the attached file. Syria is at a narrow recovery window, but health-service underfunding is cutting off care just as needs, returns, disease risks, and pressure on damaged public systems are rising. Immediate bridge funding and flexible multi-year support are needed to prevent avoidable deaths, protect frontline capacity, and keep recovery from reversing into renewed humanitarian dependence. Underfunding in 2026 is already translating into reduced operational capacity and full-service suspensions across the Syria health response. The most urgent donor concern is timing: 90 underfunded sector projects’ activities ended between January – June 2026. Immediate bridge funding, flexible reprogramming, and targeted prioritization are needed to prevent a sequence of closures and service cuts.

articles.title: ‘I’ve sat at the very precipice of life’: Clarke Carlisle on gambling, depression – and survival
articles.description: The former professional footballer has struggled with his mental health for most of his life. But it took five suicide attempts for him to admit how badly he wanted to end it. He talks about how he turned the corner – and his hopes for his new post with the charity Mind ‘How are you?” I ask Clarke Carlisle. Usually when you meet people it’s a nicety. Not with Carlisle. He smiles ecstatically. “I’m incredibly well, thank you. Yeah, really, really good,” says the former footballer and incoming chair of the mental health charity Mind. “I have been consistently well – not just stable, but well – for three or four years now.” Few people understand what it is to be mentally unwell quite like Carlisle does. And few understand what recovery means like he does. “It doesn’t happen by accident. Once you get stable that’s not the end of the journey. And that seems to be the MO of our society these days. You do something, you go into hospital and they patch you up, then send you on your way. And that’s the same with mental health. You might get some pills, have a counselling session, you might have a hug and a chat with someone, and they think that’s the end of the journey. And it’s not.” Continue reading...

articles.title: South Sudan: Rapid Ebola Virus Disease Knowledge Assessment in High-Risk Areas, July 2026
articles.description: Countries: South Sudan, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda Source: REACH Initiative Please refer to the attached file. Key Messages • Despite widespread awareness of EVD, findings indicate some respondents do not believe outbreaks are occurring in neighbouring countries, as well as relatively low levels of risk perception, especially in Juba. • Health workers and the radio seemed to be the most widely used and trusted sources of health information, but qualitative information suggests more remote communities may not have access to either. • Respondents seemed able to recall some common symptoms of EVD, but both survey findings and qualitative data indicate a widespread desire for additional information.

articles.title: Why pulses could play a bigger role in healthy and sustainable diets
articles.description: A narrative review finds that pulses may support gut and metabolic health through their fiber, protein, phytochemicals, and interactions with the gut microbiota, while offering a lower environmental footprint than many animal protein sources. Human evidence is strongest for selected cardiometabolic outcomes, while many microbiome and fermentation-related benefits remain supported mainly by animal and laboratory studies.
